reason: A is the 'Teaming and networking' section itself. B discusses application-layer computer networking, a different topic.

A is about Python logging, not exception chaining. B shows re-raising with `raise ... from e` to keep the original exception as cause.

A explains Turing's 1950 test as measuring intelligent behavior indistinguishable from humans. B likewise explains the Turing Test as an operational definition of intelligence based on indistinguishability.

A is the packaging chapter intro that promises to discuss good use cases for ML packages. B is about choosing policy-as-code solutions, unrelated to packaging.

A is a text-only QA generator with recurrent layers, no CNN or RL. B is a multimodal RL setup combining image and text but focuses on preprocessing, not concatenating CNN features with RNN hidden states.
A explains pd.cut with a number of bins for stratification. B shows pd.cut with explicit custom bin edges and labels.
A uses nn.Embedding inside a Preprocessor with LSTM encoders. B documents nn.Embedding with a standalone example.

A covers nested-loop joins and Memoize; B covers joins and hashing. Neither mentions BRIN or Bloom filters.
A defines supervised learning as mapping inputs to outputs. B likewise defines supervised learning with examples.
A is C++ order book processing, not historical bars. B states NBBO bid/ask quotes are carried forward from the previous bar when no new event occurs.
A discusses log levels and defaults for operational logging. B shows the Python logging setup (basicConfig with filename/level) and logging errors with exc_info.
A demonstrates cross_val_score with KFold and custom scoring. B explains k-fold and cross_val_score; neither covers cross_validate.
A introduces the JSON data format, not serialization. B documents the json library with dumps/loads for serialization and deserialization.

A shows a toy Gym env's step() implementation without explanation. B documents step() and its returned tuple (observation, reward, done, truncated, info).
A is the sponge construction section and describes SHA3. B is a table of contents listing the sponge/SHA3 sections.
A uses string.punctuation in a regex without explaining it. B explains string.punctuation and shows its output.
A discusses time-varying features (holidays, weather) in time-series mapping. B's 'Time-Varying Instances' is about HTTP web objects changing over time.
A explains virtual hosting by port/IP but not discovery. B is the WSTG section enumerating applications via non-standard ports and virtual hosts.
A is C++ fstream file opening, unrelated. B uses Pillow's Image.open(filename) to read images.
A documents defaultdict(int) with examples. B only uses defaultdict(int) for word counting.
A shows a custom PyTorch C++ module with forward but a CNN, not LSTM. B builds a stacked LSTM with dense layers in Keras but not a forward-pass-only custom model.
A explains AOF every-write persistence has a heavy performance hit. B offers the fix: offload persistence to a replica so aggressive saving doesn't hurt the master.
A wires create/delete endpoints with trait bounds. B defines the SaveOne/DeleteOne traits for create/delete with user-scoping.
A reports GPT-4's rumored one trillion parameters. B gives GPT-1/2/3 sizes but says GPT-4 details are kept secret.
A is a TOC listing memory management chapters. B names the section covering debugging commands and memory manipulation.
A introduces LLMs used by both attackers and defenders but without details. B details offensive (AI-crafted attacks) and defensive (phishing/threat detection) uses.
A is the concurrency/parallelism chapter covering OS threads and std::thread. B explains concurrency vs parallelism conceptually with no OS-thread coverage.
A walks through creating an EC2 key pair and connecting via ssh -i. B briefly lists key-pair creation and chmod 400 but no ssh command.
A details stacking and mentions random forest as an ensemble component. B introduces bagging/stacking and explains random forest.
A advises canonicalization and checking dot-dot-slash UTF-8 alternate representations. B gives generic traversal defenses (realpath, basename) without encoded/double-encoding coverage.
A is about dumping LLVM IR via a debugger, not a parser's AST. B mentions a formatted debug print of the parse result but without implementation.
A mentions big data in smart cities at a high level without concrete ML projects. B gives real ML+OR projects (London bike sharing, waste-bin sensors, bus-route redesign).
